example.answer: Angles are 36.87°, 53.13° and 90°, the perimeter is 12 and the area is 6.
example.problem: A triangle has sides a = 3, b = 4 and c = 5. Find the angles, the perimeter and the area.
steps: Check the triangle inequality: 3 + 4 = 7 > 5, 3 + 5 = 8 > 4, and 4 + 5 = 9 > 3, so a triangle exists.
Angle A by the law of cosines: cos A = (b² + c² − a²) ÷ 2bc = (16 + 25 − 9) ÷ 40 = 0.8, so A = 36.87°.
Angle B by the law of cosines: cos B = (a² + c² − b²) ÷ 2ac = (9 + 25 − 16) ÷ 30 = 0.6, so B = 53.13°.
Angle C = 180° − 36.87° − 53.13° = 90°. It is a right triangle.
example.title: Three sides 3, 4, 5

faqs.a: Three independent measurements, with at least one of them a side. SSS, SAS, ASA and AAS all work. Two angles alone are not enough, because they describe the shape but not the size — that triangle could be any scale.
faqs.q: What is the minimum I need to know to solve a triangle?

faqs.a: Because of the triangle inequality: the sum of any two sides must exceed the third. With sides 2, 3 and 10, the two short sides (2 + 3 = 5) cannot span the long side (10), so the triangle cannot close.
faqs.q: Why does the solver reject some side lengths?

faqs.a: Use the law of sines when angles and sides are paired up, like ASA or AAS: a ÷ sin A = b ÷ sin B = c ÷ sin C. Use the law of cosines when you know three sides (SSS) or two sides with the angle between them (SAS).
faqs.q: When should I use the law of sines instead of the law of cosines?

faqs.a: It uses only the three sides. First find the semiperimeter s = (a+b+c) ÷ 2, then the area is √(s(s−a)(s−b)(s−c)). It is exact, and it works for any triangle, including ones where the height would be awkward to measure.
faqs.q: How does Heron's formula find area without a height?

formula.label: Law of cosines (sides)
formula.note: Use when you know two sides and the angle between them.

formula.label: Law of cosines (angles)
formula.note: Use when you know all three sides and want an angle.

formula.expr: a ÷ sin A = b ÷ sin B = c ÷ sin C
formula.label: Law of sines
formula.note: Use when you know two angles and a side.

formula.label: Heron's formula (area)
formula.note: Finds the area from the three sides alone.

howItWorks: A triangle is fully determined by three independent measurements, as long as they are the right three. SSS means three sides, SAS means two sides with the angle trapped between them, and ASA means two angles with the side trapped between them. Each case unlocks the missing pieces with a different law.

With SSS, the law of cosines rearranges to give each angle from the three sides, and the third angle comes from 180° minus the other two. With SAS, the law of cosines gives the unknown side first, and then the problem becomes SSS. With ASA, the third angle is 180° minus the two you know, and the law of sines stretches the known side into the other two.

Before any of that, the solver checks the triangle inequality: the sum of any two sides must be longer than the third side. If it is not, no triangle can exist with those measurements, and the solver tells you instead of giving a nonsense answer. Once all three sides are known, the perimeter is their sum and the area comes from Heron's formula, which needs no height.
intro: Give any three matching pieces of a triangle — three sides (SSS), two sides and the angle between them (SAS), or two angles and the side between them (ASA) — and this solver finds everything else: all three sides, all three angles, the perimeter and the area, with each step shown.

mistakes.text: Sides 2, 3 and 10 look like numbers you can plug in, but 2 + 3 = 5 is not longer than 10, so no triangle exists. Always check that the two shorter sides add up to more than the longest side.
mistakes.title: Forgetting the triangle inequality

mistakes.text: In SAS the known angle must be the one between the two known sides. If you know sides a and b, the angle you enter has to be angle C, the one they trap. Any other angle needs the law of sines instead.
mistakes.title: Using the wrong angle in SAS

mistakes.text: The solver works in degrees. If your angle came from a calculator set to radians, 1.05 radians is 60 degrees, not 1.05 degrees — convert first or the sides will be wildly wrong.
mistakes.title: Mixing degrees and radians

mistakes.text: Angles feed into each other: rounding angle A to a whole degree before finding angle B shifts B too. Keep two or three decimals until the final answer, then round once.
mistakes.title: Rounding halfway through
